(...)” Much of the evidence we looked at measures performance on well-specified tasks that are easy to grade automatically or with a language model. If recent models have been growing more quickly on “clean” tasks than on “messy” tasks (relative to historical relative growth rates), then we may be overstating the acceleration in real-world impact. For instance, recent progress may be overfitting to the types of tasks which are included in AECI. Let h, c, n be the historical, current (Oct 2026), and no-AI counterfactual growth rates, measured in whatever units progress is roughly linear in. For AECI that's points per year: the fitted trend went from about +15 points/year before October 2025 to about +29 after. For an exponential metric (as in METR's worked example) it's the log growth rate. METR's definitions give total acceleration A = c/h ≈ 2, acceleration due to AI a = c/n, and implicitly non-AI acceleration b = n/h, with A = a·b. The "≈80%" is a claim about where n sits between h and c. The readings differ in which yardstick measures that. Reading 1: share of the slope change (additive). (c − n)/(c − h) = 0.8, so n = h + 0.2(c − h). In METR's "years of progress" units this is concrete. At A = 2, Anthropic makes about one extra historical-year of progress per calendar year, and about 0.8 of that extra year is due to AI. Without AI it would make about 1.2 historical-years per year, which implies a ≈ 1.67. This is probably what's intended. METR's illustrative chart labels the two gaps "excess growth due to AI" and "excess growth due to non-AI factors," it annotates the slope ΔAECI/Δtime, the AECI trends are fit linearly, and one interviewee framed it the same way, attributing 50–80% of the slope change to Claude. Reading 2: share of the log-acceleration (multiplicative). ln a / ln A = 0.8, so a = A^0.8 ≈ 1.74 and b = A^0.2 ≈ 1.15. This is natural if you take METR's ratio definitions literally. Since a·b = A, the logs add exactly, so this split doesn't depend on which factor you remove first. Reading 3: share of the excess multiplier. (a − 1)/(A − 1) = 0.8, so a = 1.8. It sounds natural ("AI provides 80% of the extra speedup"), but it isn't a decomposition. The non-AI share computed the same way is (b − 1)/(A − 1) ≈ 11%, so the two shares sum to 91%. An even more naive reading, a/A = 0.8, fails outright: if AI did nothing, a = 1 and you'd still get 1/A = 50%. Implied AI acceleration a (and non-AI acceleration b), holding the 80% fixed: The readings agree near A ≈ 1, because ln x ≈ x − 1 there, and they diverge as A grows. At METR's central estimate the spread is modest. In METR's own illustrative numbers (h = ln 2, n = ln 3, c = ln 9), AI's share comes out to 73%, 60%, or 46% under readings 1, 2, and 3. The same picture could be described as "a majority" or "a minority" depending on the yardstick. Why 1 versus 2 is really a modeling choice. If AI and other factors add to the growth rate (c = h + Δ_AI + Δ_other), reading 1 is the clean split. If they multiply (c = h·a·b, for example because AI multiplies the productivity of whatever headcount, compute, and data you have), reading 1 becomes order-dependent. The counterfactual "remove AI, keep the non-AI factors" gives AI the entire interaction term h(a − 1)(b − 1). A Shapley split of the same numbers (A = 2, b = 1.2) gives AI about 73%, not 80%. Reading 2 has no such ambiguity under a multiplicative model. Takeaway: a fix to how the AI Futures Model converts the research taste slope moves the filtered results slightly earlier and barely changes anything else. What changed: the taste slope is input as SDs/2025-year, but the model converted it using each trajectory’s pace of progress at present day (end of July 2026) rather than mid-2025. In trajectories that had already accelerated, like the filtered ones (1.2–1.4x the 2024–mid-2025 rate), this made the effective slope 20–30% lower than the parameter value. In typical trajectories the two rates match (median ratio 1.01). The conversion now uses the pace at mid-2025 (new parameter taste_slope_reference_date, default 2025.5). Effect: Daniel’s preset barely moves (SAR one week earlier). p(SAR by EO2027) goes from 72% to 77% (1.5x), 87% to 90% (1.7x), 88% to 92% (1.7x Nov 1, 1.2x May 1) and 95% to 96% (2x). The joint median SAR moves from Apr to Mar 2027; the other SAR medians are unchanged to the month, and TED-AI medians move up to a month earlier. The partial coding automation trajectory’s SAR moves from Jun to May 2027. The one-time-beta-decrease trajectory barely moves (still Mar 2027), because the conversion reads a mapping that excludes the beta shift (rate ratio 1.04). This appendix shows the fit behind the “TasteVal slope, AECI basis” row of the one-at-a-time table. TasteVal (arXiv 2610.06824) measures each model’s compute multiplier: the experiment compute the expert baseline needs to match the model’s final score, as a multiple of the model’s own compute budget. METR’s chart gives AECI only for Anthropic models, so each TasteVal model gets the AECI that METR’s fitted trend gives at its release date (+15 points per year before the October 7, 2025 break, +29 after; second plot). Release dates are read off TasteVal’s Figure 1. We fit log(compute multiplier) against this AECI for the 17 frontier models TasteVal fits (GPT-4 to Opus 5.5), allowing one change in slope at the model where it best fits the data (largest Chow F-statistic, as TasteVal does). The change falls at GPT-5.2 (AECI ≈ 155, December 2025), the same model as in TasteVal’s own fits against release date and ECI. Before it, the multiplier doubled every 19.5 AECI points; since then, every 7.2 points (90% CI 5.4–9.0 from resampling the 11 post-break models). As a check, the same fit against release date reproduces TasteVal’s 3.0-month doubling time, which is about 7.2 points at 29 AECI points per year. A continuous kinked line gives 6.7 points per doubling. Using METR’s measured AECI for the six Anthropic models instead of the trend values gives 7.9, and fitting those six models alone, without a break, gives 5.6. +2 Eli Lifland , Brendan Halstead , Daniel Kokotajlo , and 3 others Nov 10, 2026 306 90 68 Share We want to get this post out quickly given the urgency of the topic. It’s possible that there are some errors in the modeling, but we think it’s very unlikely that they undermine the high level conclusions. We would love to be corrected on any mistakes we made. METR recently estimated that Anthropic is now making AI progress about twice as fast as its historical rate (they would not be surprised by anything from 1.3x to 3x), and guessed that “perhaps ≈80%” of the current acceleration is due to AI. If they’re right, that implies an AI-driven acceleration that is 5 months ahead of the AI 2027 scenario . This level of acceleration due to AI is very unexpected. Previously, Daniel, the most bullish of us, assigned a 50% chance of Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) 1 before 2029 . SAR is roughly the point at which a company would rather fire all their human researchers and rely solely on automated AI researchers than have a team of the best human researchers in the world with no AIs. 2 Now, all of us forecast that Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will likely arrive at some point in 2027 (assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown). 3 We also predict a 35-65% chance that Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI), AIs that can automate all white-collar work, will arrive before 2028. While there were many factors and sources of evidence that influenced us, the single biggest source was the METR report. 4 . If SAR is coming in 2027, it is incredibly urgent to pause or substantially ‘pace’ frontier AI development, with the ideal being an industry-wide pause followed by an international agreement . Companies are not on track to align a SAR, and using a misaligned SAR to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) will put us in an extremely bad position. Additionally, if we train SAR in the near future, China will probably be able to steal the training recipe and maybe even the model weights ( more ). 5 We estimate that METR’s report implies a 1.7x AI-attributable acceleration in the pace of progress today, relative to historical levels. This surprises our model; we made our most recent timelines forecasts less than three months ago, and even the most aggressive model-based distribution (Daniel’s) assigned less than 4% to the pace of progress being sped up by at least 1.7x in November 2026. 6 1.7x AI-attributable acceleration is a bigger deal than it may seem; e.g., it’s a much bigger deal than making employees 1.7x more productive . We focus in this post primarily on forecasting when Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will arrive. We also discuss Top-Expert-Dominating-AI (TED-AI): AIs that are better than top human experts at virtually all tasks. ( more ) In this post, we forecast SAR and TED-AI using the following approaches: Simple models: Research taste linear extrapolation : Even assuming that the recent pace of progress doesn’t accelerate further due to automation, the fact that the recent trend is above historical rates is a big update to our timelines; a linear extrapolation of the recent rate of AI progress predicts that SAR will likely be achieved by the end of 2027. Labor uplift extrapolation : An exponential extrapolation of self-reported labor uplift predicts SAR in mid-2028. In addition to not modeling automation, there are reasons to think that an exponential is too conservative. However, self-reports may be too bullish. Extrapolating Anthropic automation levels : Anthropic recently shared a graph showing how the percentage of R&D tasks at various automation levels has changed over time. Extrapolating this predicts SAR in late 2027; this method also doesn’t model speedup from automation. Extrapolating software R&D uplift per unit of ECI : AI software R&D uplift must have recently been increasing by a larger factor with each ECI point. If we linearly extrapolate the rate at which this “factor of extra uplift per ECI point” is increasing, we get SAR in Dec 2027 (if we assume that the self-reported AI labor uplift chart is accurate) or July 2027 (if we assume that there was no meaningful automation 12 months ago and all the speed-up has happened after then). Tom Davidson’s toy model: Predicts superintelligence in around a year conditional on a software-only singularity, so SAR sometime in 2027. Filtered AI Futures Model (AIFM) : Keeping the existing AIFM (including parameter distributions), and filtering for trajectories that match METR’s AI-attributable pace of progress acceleration estimates. This serves 2 purposes on top of the simple extrapolations: Modeling how automation changes the rate of progress, allowing forecasting reasonably beyond SAR. Informing what parameter settings in the simple research taste extrapolation are plausible. The results of these methods: How to think about these results: The simple research taste extrapolation, which is a simplified version of the AIFM, gives July or September 2027, depending on whether you account for parameter uncertainty. Other simple models predict late 2027 to mid-2028. When conditioned on 1.7x Nov 2026 AI-attributed acceleration, the AIFM predicts a SAR median of Feb 2027. This is faster than the simple research taste extrapolation because it usually has a higher level of Sep 2026 research taste (in the median case, matching a median researcher), 7 and it accounts for further automation. When additionally conditioning on a 1.2x May 2026 AI-attributed acceleration, predictions get slower because it indicates a lower rate of growth than is typical when only conditioning on 1.7x in Nov. We then explore hypotheses for why the AI Futures Model was wrong , including parameter adjustments and modeling changes. The analysis is highly preliminary, and we were unable to come to strong conclusions. Our top candidates for what explains where we went wrong are: Near-AC coding skills result in more AI R&D uplift than we anticipated . This could explain the combination of ~1.7x AI-attributable acceleration in Nov and (very roughly) ~1.2x in May, without AIs already having high enough research taste to contribute to the acceleration. In this case, the gradual acceleration no longer implies a low research taste slope, so steeper slopes and faster taste-driven takeoffs are more likely. Skills besides coding and research taste (the two included in the AIFM), e.g., data generation, are driving acceleration. This potentially would have similar implications to the above bullet. But it’s unclear. Conversion of uplift to pace of progress is too conservative. I.e., we modeled diminishing returns to AI research effort too harshly. This would point toward a faster takeoff. Because the distributions of the time until SAR and of the time from SAR to TED-AI both have long right tails, the difference of the medians is typically larger than the median of the difference, so subtracting the two columns tends to overstate the median time between the two milestones. In METR’s recent assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic , they estimate that, over the past year, AI R&D progress has accelerated by ~2x relative to the trend before Oct 2025. METR estimates that ~80% of current acceleration is downstream of AI (as opposed to other factors), which implies a 1.7x acceleration due to AI (1.67–1.74x depending on how the 80% is read; see appendix ). 9 Both of these estimates rely significantly on evidence METR wasn’t able to share: METR says that “Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions”, which makes it difficult to know exactly what the 2x and 80% estimates are based on. The 2x acceleration figure is partially based on evidence METR was allowed to share: the following graph, depicting benchmark scores recently growing at roughly twice the historical rate. The 80%/1.7x estimates have no comparable public support. This estimate is produced by fitting trendlines to the performance of models as judged by AECI, Anthropic’s internal version of Epoch’s Capabilities Index ( ECI ). The trend fitted from data points after Oct 2025 has 1.9x the slope of the trend fitted from data points before Oct 2025. This was the best-fitting breakpoint (i.e., it was chosen to have the best fit to the data and it matched data better than fitting a one-time jump ). Since the accelerated trendline is an average of the progress over the last year, and we should expect AI R&D acceleration to increase over time, it’s plausible that the instantaneous acceleration right now is even faster. Regarding the acceleration getting faster over time, METR says: The rate of growth could be undergoing continuous acceleration, e.g. hyperbolic growth. While we do not see clear evidence of this in the AECI trends, there is other evidence that makes this seem more plausible which Anthropic redacted. If growth is hyperbolic, we are likely underestimating instantaneous acceleration and substantially understating acceleration in the near future. Regarding AIs’ contributions over time, METR says: We believe AI’s contribution has grown relatively more important over time. The AECI data points that had previously been released by Anthropic seemed best explained by a one-time jump at Mythos rather than a change in slope. However, with the new AECI data points from the METR report, it looks like the post-Mythos slope is now more clearly higher than the pre-Mythos one. Given the redactions, how much to update on METR’s report depends heavily on how much one trusts the redacted analysis by METR’s researchers (more discussion of this below ). This is a very unfortunate situation. We aren’t sure what reasons Anthropic gave internally for redacting all of this important information, but we are very skeptical that Anthropic is fairly assessing the costs and benefits from an impartial perspective. We strongly urge Anthropic to release enough information such that external observers can make a complete assessment. In the Fable 5.2 system card , Anthropic have not added much clarity, with the following quote being ambiguous as to whether they agree with the METR report’s estimate; they only specifically claim that “Claude Mythos 5.2” (which does not seem like the internal frontier Model 4) “ does not double the internal rate of overall aggregate progress in AI research and development.” Full quote here: Our estimates of both the degree of acceleration and the attribution to AI are uncertain, so our determination that Claude Mythos 5.2 does not cross the RSP threshold reflects a holistic judgment that, given its shortcomings and limitations, it does not double the internal rate of overall aggregate progress in AI research and development (relative to an unassisted counterfactual). We will discuss overall trends in acceleration in a future report. It seems that many people aren’t tracking how big of a deal 1.7x AI-attributable pace of progress acceleration is, often conflating it with a weaker form of uplift. METR describes a 1.7x acceleration of overall AI progress (due to AI uplift). This is saying the entire company is making 1.7x as much progress as it was before. Software R&D and research labor are only parts of the company, and inputs into overall progress. Because AI progress also depends on other factors, like compute, you should expect a 1.7x acceleration in individual inputs like software R&D or research labor to translate into less than a 1.7x acceleration in overall progress. Labor uplift is how much faster researchers are getting work done due to AI assistance. It’s as if the researchers read, write, talk, and think that much faster. According to the METR report, an informal poll of Anthropic researchers yielded an estimate of 12x – though that’s just self-reports, which may be biased. AI software R&D uplift is how much faster software progress is going with the AIs in present day than it would be without them. It is much lower than labor uplift because compute is an important input to software R&D. Imagine, for example, that your researchers get work done 12x faster, but you only have the same amount of GPUs as before. You can’t do 12x as many experiments, at least not with the same compute budget; you have to economize. Pace of progress acceleration is how much faster AI progress is advancing in present day, compared to a baseline reference period ( in Anthropic’s case , the baseline is “the fastest rate of extended progress we’ve observed in the absence of significant AI contributions to AI R&D”). It is usually much lower than AI software R&D uplift because (a) it is subject to diminishing returns to more software R&D and (b) it includes compute scaling. The compute scaling point is simple: Part of the reason why modern AIs are smarter than older AIs is literally that they are bigger, trained longer, etc. More compute goes in, more capability comes out. As AI companies build more datacenters they unlock the ability to make larger AIs and train them longer. Since overall progress comes partly from software R&D and partly from compute scaling, a doubling in software R&D will cause less than a doubling in overall progress. To expand on the diminishing returns point: AI software progress in general is subject to diminishing returns; the low-hanging fruit gets picked first, and to keep finding better and better algorithms requires exponentially more investment (more and bigger experiments, more and smarter researchers thinking for longer, etc.). Historically, the AI industry has scaled up R&D investments in a way that’s roughly cancelled out these diminishing returns. But the point here is, to get two years of research progress in one year, you have to more than double the AI software R&D uplift. (See also this Thomas Kwa tweet , this Ryan Greenblatt tweet , and Ajeya Cotra’s Substack for similar points.) As an analogy, imagine AI progress as a car driving uphill. The speed of the car is analogous to the speed of overall AI progress. Right now it’s roughly twice as fast as before. The engine is research effort. AI software R&D uplift means that there is more effective labor going into making algorithmic progress. The hill gets steeper as you go. As the easy algorithmic improvements get used up, it takes more research effort to continue progress at the same rate. To make the car go twice as fast, the engine has to work more than twice as fast, because of the hill getting steeper. On top of this, to make the engine work twice as fast, the AI needs to make humans more than twice as productive, because progress is also dependent on compute, which hasn’t significantly accelerated. 10 AI 2027 predicted 2x AI R&D uplift in Dec 2026; as argued above , this would imply a substantially lower pace of progress than the 1.7x AI-attributable pace of progress that METR’s estimates imply for Nov. So when exactly did AI 2027 predict a 1.7x pace of progress over baseline? We created this trajectory by modifying a few key parameters until it roughly matched AI 2027. In that trajectory, 1.7x acceleration over the 2024.0–2025.5 rate of progress happens in roughly April 2027. 11 So by this metric, we are ~5 months ahead of schedule. See below for a graph tracking these 2 quantities throughout the trajectory, as well as coding labor uplift (coding labor uplift is higher than overall AI R&D labor uplift, which unfortunately isn’t tracked in the AIFM): Modeling Operationalization We condition this section on there being a genuine 1.7x acceleration over the 2024-2025.5 rate of progress (we also test 1.5x and 2x), as of Nov 1. We discuss uncertainty about whether it might be slower or faster below . We focus primarily on forecasting the median arrival date of Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR), and the chance of it arriving by the end of 2027. In the AI Futures Model (AIFM) and in this writeup, a SAR is operationalized as : A SAR is an AI that, if dropped into an AGI project in present day, would be as good at research taste as the project would be if there were only human researchers, who were each made as competent at research taste as the top researcher. 12 The SAR must also qualify as an Automated Coder (AC), i.e., be able to fully automate coding in the AGI project. [By research taste, we mean the ability to select research directions and experiments, and interpret their results.] It’s a somewhat stronger condition than AI R&D parity , the point at which the company would rather fire their human researchers than fire their AIs, because the research taste must be at the level of the top human rather than the average. 13 If one wishes not to rely on our abstraction of research taste, then you can think of our SAR arrival dates as upper bounds for when AI R&D parity will be reached. We discuss forecasts of capability levels above SAR to some extent, but we focus primarily on SAR because (a) we think SAR might already represent a “point of no return” (more below ) and (b) forecasting post-SAR milestones involves positing a translation between AI R&D and general capabilities, which introduces more complexity. (You may wish to skip this section and go to the next 2 if you’re interested in the simplest extrapolations.) Here’s a simple method for forecasting when SAR will arrive: Determine how good AIs’ research taste is currently. Determine how quickly research taste improves as AIs get generally more capable (where general capabilities are measured by Anthropic’s internal version of ECI , the AECI). Linearly extrapolate the recent, accelerated AECI trend until top-human-level research taste is reached. This is a conservative method, because it assumes the recent trend merely continues, rather than bending upward due to increasing AI R&D acceleration. In fact, increasing AI R&D acceleration seems plausible: METR’s bottom-line view is that there is “significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration over the coming year.” This method doesn't depend on modeling future AI R&D acceleration, so on that dimension it errs late. This forecasting method does not require that the acceleration has been AI-attributable, just that the acceleration persists. 14 We’ll treat “Model 4,” internally deployed in Sep 2026, as the starting point. 15 We’ll use METR’s estimates of AECI for Model 4 and recent AECI slope, and convert this trend to research taste using Daniel’s median parameters for the AI Futures Model from Aug 2026. This predicts SAR arrives in Nov 2027, about 14 months after Model 4. Daniel’s parameters predict Model 4’s research taste is about −3.5 SD. SAR requires +3.09 SD, or 99.9th percentile research taste. With Daniel’s taste slope, each point of AECI converts to 0.2 SD of research taste (3 SDs per year of 2025 progress ÷ 15 AECI points per such year). That converts the recent trend of 29 AECI points per year to 5.8 SD of research taste per year. That covers the gap from −3.5 SD to the +3.09 SD threshold for SAR in 1.1 years. One-at-a-time parameter changes Here are some adjustments we could make to the above parameters: Use the old AECI slope, rather than the recent one. (This is what this simple method would have told us, before updating on the 2x overall acceleration.) Raise the Model 4 research taste to −1 SD or +1 SD, because it’s strange that it would be so low given the 1.7x AI-attributed acceleration. (In the filtered trajectories from the AIFM analyzed below, the median on Sep 25 is −0.3 to +0.2 SDs.) Use Eli’s taste slope instead of Daniel’s. Use the taste slope implied by TasteVal , a recent benchmark that measures one operationalization of research taste: how much experiment compute is required for AIs to make a given amount of research progress (on measurable tasks). The results are below. Each line/row changes one input and keeps the others at the base values. We can learn a few things from these variations. As long as the recent AECI trend persists, it’s hard to get SAR into late 2028: even Eli’s taste slope, which is lower than Daniel’s, only pushes SAR back 4 months from November 2027 to March 2028. Only reverting to the pre-acceleration AECI slope yields a SAR date in late 2028. If we’re slightly less conservative and update on Model 4 having better research taste than Daniel’s parameters suggest (given the observed AI-attributed acceleration), it’s pretty easy to get into mid or early 2027. I don’t increase it by that much in part because in this section below we can see that by filtering Daniel’s trajectories on there being 1.7x AI-attributed acceleration in Nov and 1.2x in May, the median taste slope decreases from 3 to 2.1. This is because it seems like acceleration has been growing slower than the AIFM would generally predict. 16 The Monte Carlo gives a median SAR date of July 2027, with 65% of draws reaching SAR by the end of 2027 and 84% by the end of 2028. This is earlier than the Sep 2027 you get by plugging in the median inputs. 17 Here are the full results: Labor uplift extrapolation Below we extrapolate Anthropic staff’s self-reported labor uplift based on the METR report: We extrapolate an exponential in (uplift - 1) rather than uplift, because it both makes more sense conceptually (you can’t have an uplift <1) and it better fits the data. What labor uplift corresponds to SAR? A SAR has the same effect as raising all researchers up to the taste of the best researcher, while at minimum fully automating coding. For research taste, this means that the uplift is at a minimum the difference between the top researchers’ value of labor and the average (importantly, not median) researcher’s value of labor. Perhaps this is around 100x. 18 Then we should account for complementarity between AI and humans; perhaps that brings us up to around 500x. The coding uplift will probably be quite high, given that AIs’ coding skills are currently well ahead of their research taste. However, my guess is that it’s harder to get very high uplift values in coding than in taste. Let’s say that it’s around 2,000x. The true value should be in between; perhaps these combine to about 1,000x on overall AI R&D labor uplift. So this method predicts SAR in around Aug 2028. This method is conservative in that it doesn’t model the effects of automation. Also, it assumes that (uplift-1) will be exponential in ECI, while I expect it to be superexponential (based on how coding uplift evolves in the AI Futures Model, and the fact that I think there is such huge variation in the human range in value of research taste labor (meaning that as more of the gains come from taste, uplift will increase faster)). However, it might be aggressive in that it takes self-reports at face value. Anthropic recently shared a graph showing how the percentage of R&D tasks at various automation levels has changed over time: Here is what each automation level means: My best guess is that SAR comes when nearly all tasks are AL5. Via a logistic extrapolation and an assumption that each automation level begins registering ~7 months after the previous (unfortunately, based on little data), we can get this forecast: Assuming SAR comes when 95% of tasks are AL5, this predicts SAR in Nov 2027. This method is conservative in that it doesn’t take into account the effects of automation. Of course, there is high uncertainty, especially around (a) how far AL5 will lag behind AL4 and (b) how the percentage of tasks that are AL5 relates to when SAR is achieved. Ajeya Cotra has a toy model of future acceleration here : If the first doubling of the pace took 12 months, and we’re now moving twice as fast, the next doubling might happen in just 6 months instead. Then moving 4x as fast, the next might take 3 months, then 1.5 months, etc., hitting limits within 12 months. We think there’s two important corrections to this argument, which push in opposite directions. To understand why, it’s useful to have the following model in mind: Overall “research effort” (i.e. research accomplished per unit time) is equal to [AI software R&D uplift] x [exogenous inputs]. Where exogenous inputs are some function of compute, human researchers, and data. Every doubling of cumulative research increases ECI by k points. 19 Every ECI point causes d doublings of AI software R&D uplift. (This is the same type of value that Economics of RSI refers to as “the increase in R&D effort per additional unit of ECI”. 20 ) This has been approximately 0 for most of AI history (since AI hasn’t helped with AI R&D) but now seems to be above 0. If dk>1, a doubling of cumulative research more than doubles research effort, and progress can accelerate even holding exogenous inputs fixed. Returning to Ajeya’s model, the two concerns are: The toy model effectively assumes that the exogenous inputs were constant, and assumes that the growth of [AI software R&D uplift] was large enough to both overcome diminishing returns and to increase the rate of ECI/y by 1.7x. However, in reality, the research produced during 2026 was due to a combination of an increase in the growth rate of [AI software R&D uplift] and the normal growth of exogenous inputs. The fact that exogenous inputs still grew at their normal rate cancelled out a lot of the diminishing returns, which means that the growth rate of AI software R&D uplift needed to increase somewhat less in order to achieve the 1.7x increase in ECI/y. (Relative to how much it would have had to increase without the ‘normal’ growth in exogenous inputs.) Taking this into account, we will infer lower values of dk, and dk>1 is less likely. But on the other hand, d (the number of doublings of AI software R&D uplift per ECI point) must recently have been increasing, because it used to be approximately 0 (when AI didn’t help with AI R&D) and now it’s non-0. And there’s a decent argument to expect d to continue increasing until full automation of AI R&D, because AI is becoming more and more important for AI R&D, so increasing its intelligence will be more important for productivity. (See here for a longer explanation.) Taking both these into account, my current guess is that dk is probably approaching 1. Probably a bit less right now, but d seems likely to increase and soon tip things over so that dk>1 and growth compounds without further exogenous inputs. But it's not clear what time-scale this will happen on. To nevertheless try to extrapolate, let’s try to project d into the future. I’ll assume that it will keep growing at its current slope 21 until it reaches twice its current value, at which point it stays constant. I will infer d’s historical value and growth rate under the assumptions that: AI is currently increasing the pace of progress to 1.7x its historical rate. Software efficiency has historically increased 10x/y while exogenous inputs have been growing 2x/y. This lets us infer the value of k. 22 I will make a few different assumptions about historical AI R&D uplift which will be enough to constrain d’s past trajectory. In the graph below, the y-axis depicts dk, so it’s easy to see when compounding growth becomes possible. In this graph, the circles mark 45x AI software R&D uplift as an estimate of SAR’s uplift. (The same one that would be implied by the uplift numbers in the labor uplift section above. 23 ) The estimate here that’s most grounded in data is line C, which suggests SAR in Dec 2027. 24 I’d also like to give some weight to assumptions A and B, which assume that AI only recently started significantly accelerating the pace of progress, and which suggest SAR in June and July of 2027 respectively. Here’s how SAR estimates from B and C vary with different AI-attributed starting accelerations: 25 A possible concern is that these models might be conservative by assuming linear growth in d, whereas we might expect growth to spike more aggressively as the fraction of automated tasks approaches 1 and everything gets unbottlenecked quickly. Tom Davidson wrote up a toy model of acceleration here . He describes an extremely similar trajectory to Ajeya’s original model, but his numbers don’t come from observing past progress but instead from parameters estimated in this post . 26 We haven’t formed an independent impression of what the best parameter choice is (though the AIFM has an implicit view). But Tom’s bottom line being consistent with our modeling (superintelligence around a year from now, SAR presumably before then) gives us a bit more confidence. That said, Tom says that “progress (...) may instead fizzle out” and that he was “somewhat aggressive with the numbers”, so his median may be slower. The same plots but for TED-AI: Hypotheses for why the AI Futures Model was wrong In this section, we’ll examine where our previous model-based predictions went wrong, and whether and how the model could be updated to better retrodict the recent acceleration. We’ll end up with considerations for how we should update our beliefs, conditional on accepting various hypotheses about where the AI Futures Model (AIFM) went wrong. This analysis is highly preliminary. There’s a lot to be explored here and the METR report only came out half a week ago. In the AI Futures Model, we assume that AI R&D consists of 2 skills: Coding involves implementing experiments. Research taste involves setting research directions, selecting experiments, and learning from experiments. We hypothesized when we published the model that coding would likely be automated before research taste. AIs seemed to be more advanced at coding than taste, which makes sense because coding performance is more easily verifiable. Our best guess was that when AIs fully automated coding (in the sense that the AIs alone could do all the coding as well as the humans alone), research taste would be roughly at the level of the median AGI company human researcher. The model with Daniel’s latest median parameters predicted that when an Automated Coder (AC) was developed, AI software R&D uplift would be ~2.7x and the pace of progress would be accelerated from the 2024.0-2025.5 level by ~1.25x. So naively, if we’re at a 1.7x AI-attributed pace of progress multiplier, we might think that AC has been achieved (as of Model 4). Based on the METR report and Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 system card, it seems unlikely but not totally implausible. In the Fable 5.2 system card : Anthropic says: “we have been using Claude Mythos 5.2 extensively in our own day-to-day research and engineering during the pre-release period, and it does not seem close to being able to substitute for our Research Scientists and Research Engineers.” This is the strongest evidence against AC already. On the other hand, METR surprisingly doesn’t rule out full AI R&D automation: “We are uncertain, but think it’s unlikely that [Claude Mythos 5.2] can fully automate the AI R&D process at Anthropic.” Fable 5.2, based on its AECI, likely represents “Model 3,” which is the second-most-capable internally deployed Anthropic model. Relevant interview quotes from the METR report include: Being “no longer bottlenecked on code,” “SWE acceleration… is extremely substantial.” “When people present experiments, they most often just point to an [agent scaffold] thread. Experimentation overhead is driven towards zero super fast.” There’s also the report’s assessments on automating researchers beyond coding: “We were told that R&D is accelerated primarily via AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions, but there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.” “Simply put, Anthropic tries hard to substitute researchers out for models, but researchers are still required.” 29 Note that humans could still contribute some alongside an AC: the criterion is that only the AIs could do all the coding as well as only the humans. In the report’s chart showing “Model 4 achieves >50% on all of its benchmarks” , there is a software engineering benchmark on which Model 4 gets ~52%, and another around ~75%. Surprisingly, on the 52% one, scores have been getting worse since Mythos 5. This makes me discount it substantially, but still it’s informative that Anthropic chose to include it in the AECI. The progression for the 75% one looks more reasonable; Eli thinks these benchmarks provide weak evidence against AC. (Not strong evidence, because humans might also score well under 100%.) If we’re at or slightly below AC, then we’re ahead of schedule in terms of the AI-attributed pace of progress acceleration. Why? We’ll go through the options one by one, assessing how likely they are based on the METR report and making changes to the AIFM accordingly. I’ll start with this AIFM trajectory which has AC in late Nov 2026, found by adjusting Aug 2026 coding uplift and coding uplift doubling time (we set Aug 2026 coding labor uplift to be 7x, similar to the overall AI R&D labor uplift self-reported by Anthropic staff ). 30 The trajectory has 1.04x pace of progress in May 2026, and 1.25x pace of progress in Nov 2026. Do near-AC coding skills result in more AI R&D uplift than we anticipated? Plausibly. There isn’t much evidence in the METR report either way. Perhaps you can get lots of speedup from fully automating certain types of coding, without being very bottlenecked on other tasks. We adjust the AIFM trajectory to account for this iteratively, aiming to raise the Nov 2026 pace of progress while keeping the AC date the same (by retuning the coding uplift doubling time): Doing the same with Daniel’s median research taste slope (3), rather than Eli’s (2.3), results in a final SAR date of Mar 2027. The changes made are: Increase Coding Labor Substitutability from −2 to −0.5; this is the most obvious parameter to change; it directly controls to what extent various coding tasks can substitute for each other, i.e., to what extent you can get a large speedup despite not fully automating some tasks. Increase Infinite Coding Labor Asymptote from 15 to 60; this controls the ceiling of how much AI R&D uplift you can get from automating coding alone. Decrease Slowdown from 10x less Experiment Compute from 2.8 to 1.5; this is how many times slower experiment throughput (the rate at which experiments get implemented and run, which depends on both coding labor and experiment compute) would be today with 10x less experiment compute. Lowering it means experiment compute growth accounts for less of the historical growth in experiment throughput, so a given AI R&D uplift from automating coding translates into a larger speedup relative to the historical pace of progress. This is the most consequential change, and represents the 4th percentile of our August distribution. Conclusions about when SAR and TED-AI arrive are heavily sensitive to research taste at AC: We can arbitrarily lower it while maintaining a good fit to the acceleration estimates, pushing SAR further and further back. And we can raise it to ~+2.5 SDs without the Nov 2026 acceleration getting above METR’s error bars (i.e., above 3x), moving SAR up to Dec 2026. If recent acceleration is driven by higher-than-expected uplift from near-AC coding skills, the main implication we’re tracking is that it could explain why we see ~1.7x AI-attributable acceleration in Nov and ~1.2x in May without high research taste (as in the trajectories in the table above). This allows for the possibility of high research taste slopes and fast taste-driven takeoffs, which are generally selected against when filtering for the aforementioned Nov and May observations. There are likely more implications that could be gleaned with more analysis. A few more tables of analysis are in an appendix. Research taste is better at the time of AC than anticipated (i.e., substantially better than the median AGI company researcher). Is Model 4’s research taste currently substantially above the median Anthropic researcher, despite not quite being at AC? It seems unlikely but not ruled out based on interview quotes : “Now only bottlenecked on ideas & compute, no longer bottlenecked on code.” “I’ve seen us discovering very promising directions ~entirely because people can spam 10 ideas at [agent-scaffold] and see what sticks.” It seems like Anthropic’s R&D still mostly involves humans coming up with the research ideas, based on these quotes and the absence of positive evidence. One could imagine that the AIs are a bit better than the median humans, but that humans still come up with most of the ideas because the ideas generally come from top humans (e.g., research leads). But it seems unlikely that they are substantially better than the median. Does a given level of research taste skill result in more AI R&D uplift than we anticipated? Likely not. For example, perhaps research taste is multi-dimensional and the dimensions are complementary. This seems unlikely to be a main driver of the pace of progress multiplier, given the evidence presented for why research taste at AC isn’t better than anticipated (i.e., there weren’t any dimensions of research taste in which Claude was reported to be particularly helpful). Are skills besides coding and research taste (as they are conceptualized in the AIFM) a large contributor to the acceleration? Plausibly. (Implies: lower research taste than we would otherwise expect). We think the biggest candidate for this is RL environment generation (or other data generation tasks). These count in some sense as coding, but the coding modeled in the AIFM is experiment implementation, not data generation. And this seems very amenable to automation. METR’s report doesn’t discuss this, including the interview quotes, which is some evidence against it being such a huge deal. But it seems plausible that it just happened to not be discussed in the publicly released quotes. Could data generation lead to a substantial AI-attributed acceleration before AC? It seems plausible that it’s at least as automatable as experiment implementation, so including it as a skill when modeling AI R&D would increase the overall level of AI-attributed acceleration. It would probably have to be significantly more automatable than coding to explain the missing acceleration on its own. 31 We don’t know of a quick fix to the AIFM to model this possibility. But let’s assume that this is the primary thing that the AIFM is missing. What would that imply about our forecasts going forward? One implication is that it could explain substantial acceleration despite poor research taste (similar to the implications of high uplift from near-AC coding skills). Otherwise, it seems unclear. Further work would be helpful for figuring out the implications of this hypothesis. We don’t know of other skills that are as strong candidates to be the missing contributor as data generation, but it’s plausible we’re just not thinking of them. Is the conversion of uplift to pace of progress in the AIFM too conservative? Plausibly. (Implies: faster takeoff). In the AIFM, we assume that every doubling in cumulative research effort results in a fixed number of doublings of software efficiency (as in the Jones model ). This is how we model “ideas getting harder to find”; more research effort is required for each successive doubling (and each doubling of software efficiency corresponds to a fixed amount of ECI points). This seems to roughly fit historical progress, in the very loose sense that we’ve seen approximately steady growth in compute and labor investment into AI software R&D, and roughly exponential increases in software efficiency. However, this model has failed (perhaps twice now) to predict accelerations in ECI amid steady training compute growth — once in 2024 with the introduction of reasoning models , and again in 2026 as reported by METR. 32 We attempt to crudely account for this by allowing beta, the parameter governing the extent to which ideas get harder to find as more ideas are found, to change over time. If we start with Daniel’s median parameters, then we add a one-time decrease in beta in Oct 2025, we can get a trajectory with AC in late Dec 2026, ~1.7x acceleration in May 2026 and ~2.1x in Nov. This matches METR’s assessment of the overall Nov pace of progress acceleration fairly well, though it seems a bit aggressive for May. Also, as of Nov 2026, ~67% of the acceleration is attributable to AI. This seems well within the error bounds of METR’s 80% assessment. With Daniel’s default +3 SDs/2025-year research taste slope and +0 research taste SDs at AC, this results in SAR in Mar 2027, and TED-AI and ASI in Apr 2027. To make it easier to understand the implications of this hypothesis, we compared its forecasts against some representative trajectories from the above methods, matching their Sep 25 taste and taste slope: 33 It seems like this hypothesis predicts slightly faster SAR and much faster post-SAR takeoff than the other methods. The faster takeoff is explained by the weaker “ideas getting harder to find” effect. Note that we can probably get a similar non-AI-attributable acceleration via changing the “a” parameter in our model rather than beta, without getting the update toward faster takeoff. We haven’t had a chance to look deeply into this. Above, we’ve taken the 1.7x acceleration at face value and reasoned about its implications. But is the acceleration even real? Or is it possible that it’s even larger? This is tough to analyze because we don’t have the information we need. As METR says, “ Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions .” However, we can at least consider METR’s own stated caveats: This estimate is given with high uncertainty; we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate. (...) We would be surprised if the true evolution of benchmark scores (e.g. as measured by an improved version of AECI) showed no acceleration or acceleration above 3x “Our best guesses as to how we might be underestimating acceleration: We may have missed recent further acceleration. The rate of growth could be undergoing continuous acceleration, e.g. hyperbolic growth. While we do not see clear evidence of this in the AECI trends, there is other evidence that makes this seem more plausible which Anthropic redacted. (...) Automation could be closer than we estimated. (...) It is possible that automation is close, and leads to very rapid acceleration once human bottlenecks are removed. AECI could understate real-world capability impact. (...)” “Our best guesses as to how we might be overestimating acceleration: Non-AI factors could explain most of the acceleration. (...) Acceleration might be limited to well-specified tasks. (...) Our acceleration numbers could be overstated if the historical rate of growth was unusually low. (...)” Overall, this increases our uncertainty in both directions: the possibility of hyperbolic growth (which METR says redacted evidence made more plausible) should shorten our timelines. the possibility that acceleration is limited to well-specified tasks should lengthen our timelines. Not only in this section, but also throughout the report, METR consistently warns that its estimates are about acceleration on well-specified tasks. So it seems especially important to understand how this may affect the prospects for AI R&D automation. Quoting METR in full: Much of the evidence we looked at measures performance on well-specified tasks that are easy to grade automatically or with a language model. If recent models have been growing more quickly on “clean” tasks than on “messy” tasks (relative to historical relative growth rates), then we may be overstating the acceleration in real-world impact. For instance, recent progress may be overfitting to the types of tasks which are included in AECI. There’s a plausible story for why recent acceleration could be happening more on clean than on messy tasks. AIs are significantly better at more well-specified tasks, and improving benchmark performance on well-specified tasks is itself more well-specified than improving general across-the-board performance. So it’s plausible that AI speeds up the “performance on well-specified tasks” pace more than it speeds up the more general pace. The METR team did say that they “investigated a number of internal metrics and methodologies for measuring acceleration in key areas of the model training pipeline”, partly with the goal of gathering evidence about “[w]hether Anthropic could be overfitting to internal metrics”, with a conclusion that seemed to indicate that they didn’t think it was just overfitting. 34 A lot of the question here is whether improvements on well-specified metrics will generalize far enough to increase models’ abilities to do AI R&D, which in turn also depends on the degree to which AI R&D is a well-specified task. The fact that AI R&D (at least as measured on not-obviously-overfit well-specified tasks) is being accelerated with current models is some update towards ML being feasible to accelerate with models that are less good at non-well-specified tasks. 35 And at least some AI R&D metrics seem both very well-specified and likely to generalize quite far if models could improve them, such as pretraining loss. Overall there does seem to be a significant chance that this slows things down substantially beyond what the AIFM or simple models have accounted for, but less than 50%. A different source of uncertainty is that there’s little acceleration when looking at all models. Acceleration is limited to Anthropic, which were previously more behind other models and have recently been catching up. And preliminary numbers from the draft of a different METR team (who weren’t embedded and which don’t have private information about Anthropic) show much less of a speed-up on an ECI-like measure of progress. 36 Preliminary investigation indicates that there are many confusing reasons for these differences and our main takeaway so far is that ECI-like measures and piecewise-linear fits seem to be sensitive to minor methodological choices. 37 If the AECI chart was the only evidence we had, this kind of confusion would cause us to discount the possibility of acceleration significantly (given that our priors on such fast acceleration were low). It does still cause us to discount it a little bit. But mostly we still trust that the METR people who were embedded in Anthropic understood the limitations of ECI and piecewise-linear fits, and that their views remained supported by other evidence they had. One reason why we mostly trust the METR team is because we know many of the people at METR and think they are reasonable; another reason why we mostly trust METR here is that (if we understand correctly) the people involved had similar or longer timelines than us before the assessment, so it’s not like they went in and saw what they wanted to see – on the contrary, the conclusion they are now putting forth seems to be very different from their prior views. 38 Moreover, there are various other sources of evidence that have accumulated since our previous timelines update that seem to corroborate the overall sense that timelines are shorter than we thought. For example, the Mathopocalypse seems to be evidence of many extremely long-horizon math problems being solved autonomously by AI. Another example: People we know who work at AI companies are saying that timelines are indeed very short and that RSI is imminent, even more than they were before, and much more than historically (remember, when AI 2027 came out most of our friends in industry said it depicted AI capabilities growing too fast). They are saying this both in public and in private. Another example: The TasteVal data suggests that AIs may already have better research taste than we expected and that they may be improving in research taste faster than we expected. This is a qualitative argument rather than a model. It’s surprising that we’re already getting 1.7x acceleration, because the models still have significant weaknesses compared to humans, and we had expected these weaknesses to significantly bottleneck progress. Regardless of how we reconcile this, you update towards Superhuman AI Researchers being much closer in time
